DATA BREACH GDPR Telecom

Odido Data Breach: 6.2 Million Dutch Telecom Customers Exposed via Compromised Salesforce CRM — The Anatomy of a Social Engineering Masterclass

February 17, 2026 20 min read TheHGTech Security Research Expert Level 
        <img src="/images/articles/odido-data-breach-6m-2026.png"
            alt="Odido Data Breach 6.2 Million Dutch Customers Salesforce CRM Technical Analysis"
            class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <!-- STATS -->
        <div class="stat-grid">

        <!-- EXECUTIVE SUMMARY -->
        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — BLUF:</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.75rem;"><strong>What:</strong> Dutch telecommunications provider
                <strong>Odido</strong> (formerly T-Mobile Netherlands) suffered one of the largest data breaches in
                Dutch history over the weekend of February 7-8, 2026. Attackers compromised the company's
                <strong>Salesforce-based customer contact management system</strong>, exfiltrating personal data of
                approximately <strong>6.2 million customers</strong>.</p>
            <p><strong>What was stolen:</strong> Names, home addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of
                birth, <strong>bank account numbers (IBANs)</strong>, and <strong>identification document
                    numbers</strong> (passport or driver's license). Passwords, call records, billing information,
                and ID document scans were NOT accessed.</p>
            <p><strong>How:</strong> The breach was facilitated through a combination of <strong>phishing and social
                    engineering attacks</strong> targeting Odido's customer service employees, resulting in
                compromised credentials that provided access to the Salesforce CRM environment.</p>
            <p><strong>Confidence Level:</strong> Confirmed | <strong>TLP:</strong> CLEAR | <strong>Source:</strong>
                Odido official statement, Dutch DPA notification, The Record, SecurityWeek, The Register</p>
        </div>

        <!-- INCIDENT TIMELINE -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> 1. Incident Timeline</h2>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Date</th>
                    <th>Event</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Feb 7-8, 2026</strong></td>
                    <td>Unauthorized access to Odido's Salesforce customer contact system detected</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Feb 8, 2026</strong></td>
                    <td>Odido terminates unauthorized access; incident response initiated with external
                        cybersecurity experts</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Feb 9, 2026</strong></td>
                    <td>Breach reported to the <strong>Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens</strong> (Dutch Data Protection
                        Authority) within 72 hours per GDPR requirements</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Feb 10, 2026</strong></td>
                    <td>Odido begins notifying affected customers via email and SMS</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>

                    <td>Media reports confirm 6.2 million customer records compromised — the breach is among the
                        largest in Dutch history</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Feb 12-14, 2026</strong></td>
                    <td>Investigation links breach to compromised Salesforce environment via phishing/social
                        engineering of customer service employees</td>
                </tr>

                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <!-- ATTACK ANALYSIS -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> 2. Attack Vector Analysis: The Social Engineering Kill Chain</h2>

        <p>The Odido breach is a masterclass in how <strong>human-centric attacks</strong> bypass even sophisticated
            technical controls. The attackers did not exploit a Salesforce zero-day or brute-force credentials. They
            manipulated people.</p>

        <h3>2.1 Reconstructed Attack Chain</h3>
        <p>Based on available reporting from Odido's own disclosures, TechZine.eu, and SalesforceBen, the following
            kill chain emerges:</p>

        <div class="attack-flow">
            <pre style="color: var(--accent-purple); margin: 0;">

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ODIDO BREACH — RECONSTRUCTED KILL CHAIN │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ │ PHASE 1: RECONNAISSANCE │ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ • Identify Odido customer service agents │ │ │ │ via LinkedIn/social media │ │ │ │ • Map internal tools (Salesforce Service │ │ │ │ Cloud identified as primary CRM) │ │ │ │ • Identify SSO/auth mechanisms │ │ │ └──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ PHASE 2: CREDENTIAL HARVESTING (Social Engineering) │ │ ┌──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐ │ │ │ • Spear-phishing emails mimicking Odido │ │ │ │ internal IT/HR communications │ │ │ │ • Fake “password reset” or “MFA reconfig” │ │ │ │ pages cloning Salesforce SSO portal │ │ │ │ • Possible voice phishing (vishing) calls │ │ │ │ impersonating IT support │ │ │ └──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ PHASE 3: INITIAL ACCESS │ │ ┌──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐ │ │ │ • Login to Salesforce Service Cloud with │ │ │ │ harvested credentials │ │ │ │ • Bypass MFA (if enabled) via: │ │ │ │ - MFA fatigue bombing (push spam) │ │ │ │ - Real-time phishing relay proxy │ │ │ │ - Stolen session token │ │ │ └──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ PHASE 4: DATA EXFILTRATION │ │ ┌──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐ │ │ │ • Use Salesforce SOQL queries or Data │ │ │ │ Loader to bulk export customer records │ │ │ │ • 6.2 million records extracted within │ │ │ │ the Feb 7-8 weekend window │ │ │ │ • Exfiltration likely via Salesforce API │ │ │ │ exports (CSV/JSON) │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ RESULT: 6.2M records including IBANs and passport numbers │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 

        <h3>2.2 Why Weekends Matter</h3>
        <p>The attackers chose a <strong>Saturday-Sunday window</strong> (Feb 7-8). This is a well-known pattern in
            data exfiltration operations:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Reduced monitoring:</strong> SOC teams are typically understaffed on weekends. Alert fatigue
                is higher.</li>
            <li><strong>Slower response:</strong> Escalation chains are longer when key decision-makers are
                off-duty.</li>
            <li><strong>Higher data export limits:</strong> Some Salesforce orgs relax API rate limits during
                off-hours.</li>
            <li><strong>Plausible cover:</strong> Batch data jobs (backups, syncs) often run on weekends, masking
                anomalous bulk exports.</li>
        </ul>

        <!-- WHAT WAS STOLEN -->

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> Critical Observation:</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem;">The combination of <strong>IBAN + Full Name + Date of Birth + Address +
                    Passport Number</strong> constitutes a complete <strong>"Identity Theft Kit."</strong> This data
                package is sufficient to:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>Open fraudulent bank accounts in the Netherlands and EU</li>
                <li>Execute unauthorized SEPA direct debits</li>
                <li>Apply for loans or credit cards using stolen identities</li>
                <li>File fraudulent tax returns</li>
                <li>Conduct SIM swap attacks to intercept SMS-based MFA codes</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <!-- SALESFORCE SECURITY -->
        <h2><i class="fab fa-salesforce"></i> 4. Salesforce CRM Security: Lessons from the Breach</h2>

        <p>This breach is not a Salesforce vulnerability. It's a <strong>Salesforce configuration and access control
                failure</strong> on Odido's part. However, it highlights systemic risks that every Salesforce
            customer should evaluate:</p>

        <h3>4.1 Common Salesforce Security Gaps</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Overprivileged Service Accounts:</strong> Customer service agents often have broader data
                access than required. A single compromised account can access millions of records if row-level
                security (Field-Level Security and Record-Level Security) is not enforced.</li>
            <li><strong>Insufficient MFA Enforcement:</strong> While Salesforce mandates MFA, organizations can
                implement it weakly (SMS-based, easily phished MFA push notifications).</li>
            <li><strong>No Bulk Export Alerts:</strong> Salesforce does not natively alert on anomalous data export
                volumes. Organizations must configure <strong>Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring</strong> (paid
                add-on) or build custom alerts.</li>
            <li><strong>Session Hijacking:</strong> Stolen session tokens bypass MFA entirely. Without IP
                restrictions on sessions, an attacker with a valid session cookie can operate from anywhere.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>4.2 Detection: SOQL Audit Query</h3>
        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-code"></i> Salesforce SOQL — Detect Anomalous Bulk Data Exports</h3>
            <pre><code class="language-sql">-- Salesforce Event Monitoring Query

– Detect unusual bulk data access from the EventLogFile

SELECT UserId, Username, ClientIp, RequestType, RecordCount, Timestamp FROM EventLogFile WHERE EventType = ‘ReportExport’ OR EventType = ‘BulkApiResult’ AND RecordCount > 10000 AND Timestamp > LAST_N_DAYS:7 ORDER BY RecordCount DESC

– Flag: Any single session exporting > 50K records – Flag: Any export from unrecognized IP range – Flag: Any export outside business hours (weekends, 22:00-06:00)

        <!-- GDPR ANALYSIS -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-gavel"></i> 5. GDPR Implications & Regulatory Exposure</h2>

        <p>The Odido breach falls squarely under the <strong>General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)</strong>. As
            a Dutch entity processing EU citizen data, Odido faces significant regulatory scrutiny.</p>

        <h3>5.1 GDPR Obligations Assessment</h3>

                    </td>
                </tr>

                    <td><strong>Art. 34 — Communication</strong></td>

                    </td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Art. 32 — Security Measures</strong></td>

                        controls adequate?</td>

                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Art. 25 — Data Protection by Design</strong></td>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-landmark"></i> Historical Precedent:</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem;">The largest GDPR fine in the Netherlands to date was
                <strong>€750,000</strong> against the Dutch Tax Administration in 2020. However, the scale of the
                Odido breach (6.2M records with financial data) and the nature of the data (IBANs, passport numbers)
                could push the AP toward a significantly higher penalty, potentially in the <strong>€10-50
                    million</strong> range based on precedents set by other EU DPAs (Ireland's €1.2B Meta fine,
                Luxembourg's €746M Amazon fine).</p>
        </div>

            reflects the industry's improved technical posture being undermined by insufficient investment in
            <strong>security awareness training</strong> and <strong>identity-centric security controls</strong>.
        </p>

        <!-- DEFENSIVE RECOMMENDATIONS -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> 7. Defensive Recommendations</h2>

        <h3>For Organizations Using Salesforce:</h3>
        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> IMMEDIATE ACTIONS:</strong>
            <ol>
                <li><strong>Audit Data Access:</strong> Review all Salesforce user profiles. Apply the
                    <strong>principle of least privilege</strong>. Customer service agents should NOT have access to
                    IBANs or identity document numbers unless explicitly required for a specific workflow.</li>
                <li><strong>Enforce Phishing-Resistant MFA:</strong> Move from SMS/push-based MFA to
                    <strong>FIDO2/WebAuthn</strong> hardware keys (YubiKey) for all Salesforce users with data
                    access.</li>
                <li><strong>Enable Shield Event Monitoring:</strong> Configure real-time alerts for bulk data
                    exports, unusual login locations, and off-hours activity.</li>
                <li><strong>IP Restriction:</strong> Lock Salesforce sessions to known corporate IP ranges. Use
                    Salesforce's <strong>Login IP Ranges</strong> and <strong>Trusted IP Ranges</strong> features.
                </li>
                <li><strong>Data Masking:</strong> Implement <strong>Salesforce Shield Platform Encryption</strong>
                    and field-level masking for sensitive fields (IBANs, government IDs).</li>
            </ol>
        </div>

        <h3>For Affected Odido Customers:</h3>
        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-user-shield"></i> CUSTOMER PROTECTION CHECKLIST:</strong>
            <ol>
                <li><strong>Monitor Bank Accounts:</strong> Check for unauthorized direct debits. Contact your bank
                    to enable alerts on all SEPA transactions.</li>
                <li><strong>Freeze Credit (if available):</strong> In the Netherlands, contact BKR (Bureau Krediet
                    Registratie) to flag your profile.</li>
                <li><strong>Beware Phishing:</strong> Expect targeted phishing emails/SMS pretending to be from
                    Odido, banks, or government agencies. Never click links in unsolicited messages.</li>
                <li><strong>Report Suspicious Activity:</strong> Use <a href="https://www.fraudehelpdesk.nl/"
                        target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Fraude Helpdesk</a> (Dutch Fraud Helpdesk) to report any
                    suspicious contact.</li>
                <li><strong>Request Identity Protection:</strong> Under GDPR Art. 82, affected individuals may be
                    entitled to compensation. Consider joining collective action efforts.</li>
            </ol>
        </div>

        <!-- YARA RULE -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-search"></i> 8. Detection Rules: Identify Phishing Infrastructure</h2>

        <div class="technical-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-code"></i> YARA Rule — Salesforce SSO Phishing Kit Detection</h3>
            <pre><code class="language-yara">rule Salesforce_SSO_Phishing_Kit_2026

{ meta: description = “Detects Salesforce SSO phishing kits used in CRM-targeted attacks like Odido breach” author = “TheHGTech Security Research” date = “2026-02-17” severity = “high” reference = “https://thehgtech.com/articles/odido-data-breach-6m-2026.html” tlp = “white”

strings:
    // Salesforce login page cloning indicators
    $sf_login1 = "login.salesforce.com" nocase
    $sf_login2 = "*.my.salesforce.com" nocase
    $sf_login3 = "sfdc_oauth" nocase
    $sf_login4 = "SalesforceIdentity" nocase

    // Credential harvesting indicators
    $harvest1 = "action=\"https://" nocase  // External form action
    $harvest2 = "password" nocase
    $harvest3 = "username" nocase

    // Phishing kit infrastructure
    $kit1 = "XMLHttpRequest" nocase
    $kit2 = "fetch(" nocase
    $kit3 = "/collect" nocase
    $kit4 = "/exfil" nocase
    $kit5 = "telegram.org/bot" nocase  // Telegram exfil
    $kit6 = "discord.com/api/webhooks" nocase  // Discord exfil

    // Anti-analysis
    $anti1 = "headless" nocase
    $anti2 = "puppeteer" nocase
    $anti3 = "PhantomJS" nocase

condition:
    filesize < 1MB and
    (
        // Salesforce login clone + credential harvesting
        (2 of ($sf_login*) and 2 of ($harvest*) and $harvest1) or
        // Salesforce branding + exfiltration channel
        (1 of ($sf_login*) and 1 of ($kit*) and 1 of ($harvest*)) or
        // Phishing kit with anti-analysis + credential theft
        (1 of ($anti*) and 2 of ($kit*) and 2 of ($harvest*))
    )

} 

        <!-- LESSONS -->
        <h2><i class="fas fa-graduation-cap"></i> 9. Strategic Lessons & Industry Forecast</h2>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-binoculars"></i> TheHGTech Forecast:</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem;">The Odido breach signals a <strong>paradigm shift</strong> in enterprise
                targeting. Attackers are increasingly bypassing hardened infrastructure (firewalls, WAFs, EDR) by
                targeting the <strong>SaaS layer</strong> — specifically CRM platforms (Salesforce, HubSpot,
                ServiceNow) that aggregate the most sensitive customer data with the broadest access surface
                (hundreds of agents, contractors, partners). Expect 3-5 major CRM-based breaches in H1 2026.</p>
        </div>

        <h3>Key Takeaways:</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>SaaS ≠ Secure:</strong> Shared responsibility means your Salesforce org is only as secure as
                your configuration and your employees' phishing resistance.</li>
            <li><strong>Data Minimization Saves You:</strong> If Odido's CS agents didn't need access to IBANs and
                passport numbers, those fields should have been masked. The data that doesn't exist in the CRM can't
                be stolen from it.</li>
            <li><strong>Weekend Monitoring Gaps Kill:</strong> Invest in 24/7 SOC coverage or automated playbooks
                that trigger on bulk export anomalies regardless of time.</li>
            <li><strong>Identity is the New Perimeter:</strong> With SaaS, the traditional network perimeter is
                irrelevant. Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2), Conditional Access Policies, and continuous session
                validation are the new firewalls.</li>
        </ol>
